strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely new problem class: offline and online min-max optimization with non-smooth submodular-concave objectives. Prior work (Adibi et al. 2022 on convex-submodular, Mualem et al. 2024 on integer min-max) does not cover this setting, so the 'first study' claim appears well-founded and the paper carefully distinguishes itself from convex-submodular cases.

The theoretical development is coherent and mostly careful: the reduction to the Lovász extension (Lemma 2.7), the analysis of when saddle points of f exist and coincide with solutions of the relaxed problem (Propositions 2.10–2.11, with honest counterexamples in Appendix B), and the rounding argument via uniform threshold sampling are all handled rigorously.

The proofs in Appendix C are complete and contain non-trivial technical work beyond a routine combination of known results, e.g., the auxiliary-sequence argument (following Nemirovski et al.) to bound the sup over z in expectation for the duality gap (equations (45)-(50)), and the online analysis tracking the moving saddle point via path length.

The online duality gap O(√(N(1+P̄))) result is consistent with established behavior in online optimization, and the discussion of relaxing the four-query-per-function-change assumption (Appendix D, Remarks D.3-D.4) with the extra O(NV) error term is a useful and honest refinement.

Experiments cover both the offline and online regimes across three applications (adversarial segmentation offline/online, adversarial semi-supervised clustering offline/online), with hyperparameters reported, multiple runs (variance ~1e-4), an explicit robustness-accuracy trade-off study versus the adversary budget ρ (Figure 9), and a comparison table against trained U-Net baselines.

Limitations are candidly acknowledged: sensitivity of accuracy and tuning to the rate of change of the cost function (Appendix E.2), and the caveat that the U-Net baselines are trained and evaluated without adversaries while the comparison focuses on the strict online, adversarial, resource-constrained regime.
weaknesses: The algorithmic technique is largely a combination of established ingredients: the extragradient framework, Gaussian-smoothed two-point ZO oracles (Nesterov & Spokoiny), and subgradients of the Lovász extension (Hazan & Kale). The convergence analysis closely parallels Nesterov & Spokoiny and Nedić & Ozdaglar; the main novelty is the adaptation to the structured problem class rather than new proof techniques or fundamentally new algorithmic ideas.

The guarantee that the returned discrete pair is an ε-saddle point is weaker than it first appears: equation (19) shows D_τ(S̄_N, ȳ_N) ≤ ε where D_τ involves max_y E_τ[f(S̄_N, y)] — i.e., the gap holds only in expectation over the uniformly sampled threshold τ, not for the worst-case (or even the realized) discrete set. The practical significance of an expected-over-τ saddle point guarantee deserves more discussion.

The central assumption that a saddle point of f exists, with condition (10) (min over the hypercube equals min over vertices for the max), is restrictive and generally not verifiable a priori. Proposition 2.11 gives sufficient conditions (e.g., ζ(x) is itself a Lovász extension, or common vertex minimiser) that are somewhat ad hoc, and the experiments never verify whether (10) holds for the applied problems (segmentation, clustering).

Per-iteration cost is 6n function evaluations (Remark 3.3) and total complexity O(nm²ε⁻²) scales linearly in the ground-set size; all experiments are small-scale (50×50 images, 40-50 point clustering), so scalability to realistic segmentation or clustering problems is not demonstrated. The claimed real-time 60 fps operation is only shown on these tiny instances.

The comparison in Table 1 is methodologically uneven: the U-Net baselines are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 is 'robust by design' and evaluated under adversarial perturbations. Although the paper frames the comparison as evaluating the strict online adversarial regime, the headline claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' trained U-Nets is not an apples-to-apples result and could overstate practical significance.

The online result requires a known deterministic upper bound P̄ on the path length to set the step size h2; such a bound is generally unavailable in practice, and the paper offers only a brief justification that a trivial bound always exists. No experiment validates the O(√(N(1+P̄))) rate.

Numerous minor presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Submodluar' in Appendix B heading, 'C. Proof of Lemmas, Propositions, and Theorems' in the section title, 'minx∈{0,1}n f f L' in (30) on page 14, inconsistent bracket '∈ [0,1]' vs '[0, 1]'), an incomplete URL in the reference (Farzin et al., 2025a), and a stray '23' after the CPU specification in Appendix E. Several cited works are arXiv preprints or self-citations of the authors' own ZO line of work.

The dependence of the y-update on the Lovász extension value f^L(x,y), which itself requires n function evaluations per call, means the ZO oracle cost is tied to n; the paper argues this is optimal given Remark D.1, but an empirical ablation (e.g., t_k sensitivity, effect of n) is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem class: non-smooth submodular-concave min-max problems, in both offline and online settings, and claims (plausibly) to be the first systematic ZO treatment of this combination.

The theoretical development is careful and complete. The offline analysis (Theorem 3.2) gives an ε-saddle point guarantee with explicit hyperparameter choices, and the online analysis (Theorem 3.6) yields an O(√(N(1+P̄))) duality gap consistent with classical dynamic-regret behaviour. The appendices contain full proofs, including a non-trivial extension of the Nemirovski et al. auxiliary-sequence technique to handle the correlated oracle noise in the extragradient setting (eqs. 46-50).

The paper is honest about the subtleties: Propositions 2.10-2.11 explicitly characterise when a saddle point exists and when solving the relaxed problem (7) recovers a solution of (1), and Appendix B gives concrete examples both with and without saddle points. Appendix D carefully discusses relaxing the four-query assumption and the extra error term O(NV) that arises.

The numerical section spans four settings (offline/online segmentation, offline/online clustering) with reasonable implementation detail, hyperparameters, and an honest discussion of the adversarial budget ρ and its robustness-accuracy trade-off.

The discussion of limitations is genuine (e.g., sensitivity of accuracy to the rate of change of the cost function, per Remark D.4), and the comparison table does not hide that U-Net baselines were evaluated without adversaries.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely a synthesis of known components: the extragradient/ZO machinery is taken from Farzin et al. (2025a) and Nesterov & Spokoiny (2017), the Lovász extension subgradient oracle from Hazan & Kale (2012), and the online path-length analysis follows Zinkevich (2003). The main novelty is the combination and the bookkeeping for the set-valued variable, which reduces the incremental feel of the results.

A central applicability concern: the algorithm solves the relaxation (7) and the guarantees (Theorem 3.2, eq. 19; Theorem 3.6, eq. 26) are stated for the threshold-averaged quantity E_τ[f(S_τ, y)], i.e., for the Lovász-relaxed duality gap, not for the original integer problem (1). Recovery of a genuine discrete ε-saddle point of (1) requires the restrictive conditions of Proposition 2.11 (e.g., a common vertex minimiser or vertex minimisers of ζ). For the adversarial segmentation/clustering instances in Section 4 and Appendix E, no verification is offered that these conditions hold, so the theory may not actually certify the behaviour observed in the experiments.

The headline empirical claim that Algorithm 1 'outperforms' supervised and semi-supervised U-Nets (Table 1) is not persuasive: the U-Nets are trained and evaluated without adversaries while Algorithm 1 runs in the adversarial regime, no adversarially-trained baseline is included, and the domain is tiny synthetic 50x50 two-segment images. This comparison says more about the experimental design than about the merits of the method.

Scalability is a concern that the paper does not confront: each iteration requires ~6n function evaluations (Remark 3.3), giving O(nm²ε⁻²) total queries with a per-iteration cost linear in n. For the 2500-pixel images used, this implies ~15,000 function evaluations per iteration, which sits awkwardly with the claimed ~80 fps real-time performance; no profiling or wall-clock breakdown is provided.

The online guarantees require knowledge of an upper bound P̄ on the path length of optimal decisions to set the step sizes, and the resulting bound O(√(N(1+P̄))) is vacuous when P̄ grows linearly; the paper does not discuss how restrictive this is in practice.

Presentation has a number of loose ends: the oracle (14) is a smoothed estimate but the subgradient g_x is exact only up to the sampled chain/threshold coupling; the dependency between the threshold sampling and the function-value oracle in (8) is glossed over; several typos and notation inconsistencies (e.g., f^L_μ vs. ∇y f^L_{kμ} in (23), 'P^N_{k=0}' summation limits) reduce polish. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the experimental claims.

The 'first study' claim, while defensible in the narrow non-smooth submodular-concave setting, sits close to prior work on convex-submodular min-max (Adibi et al., 2022), submodular integer min-max (Mualem et al., 2024), and ZO extragradient min-max (Farzin et al., 2025a); the positioning could better delineate what is technically new beyond the combined setting.
